paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Marion, Ohio, took place in early February 1919, when a crowd stoned Black homes and warning placards ordered Black workers to leave the city after the murder of a white woman and an assault on another woman. An exodus of Black residents followed, and a man accused in the assault was moved out of the county jail after threats of lynching. A month later about thirty Black property-owning families were reported still living in the city.

Mrs. Clyde Scranton, a white woman of 28, was killed on the night of January 29, 1919. Her attacker or attackers clubbed her to death on the street near her home and dragged her body to an ash heap behind the Erie railroad shop, where her husband worked. On the following Sunday Mrs. Margaret Christian was assaulted, and George Washington Warner was arrested and accused of the attack.

Late on Monday night a crowd of men and boys assembled on Marion's west side. Early in the evening it chased a Black man, who escaped uninjured, and stones and bricks from the crowd broke windows in the houses of several Black families. Three hundred "vigilantes," organized for guard duty during the war, turned out because it appeared that the police and sheriff's deputies might not be able to handle the situation, and the crowd dispersed.

Warner had been placed in the Marion jail by Sheriff James Ullom, but when reports spread that a mob was headed there for him, he was put into an automobile and driven to Mount Gilead. The same dispatch also placed him in the Mansfield reformatory "following threats of lynching."

Meanwhile, placards posted in the Erie railroad roundhouse, where many Black men worked, and on the west side called on Black residents to leave the city by six o'clock at night. An exodus was under way by February 5, and the few Black people who stayed remained in their homes "behind barred doors."

Mayor A. J. Sautter closed all saloons and, with the sheriff, placarded the business district with a statement warning that people loitering on the streets would be arrested because of "the sudden danger of mob violence." The county commissioners offered a $1,000 reward in the Scranton murder, Erie railroad workers raised $1,000 for a detective, and Judge Grant C. Mouser announced a special grand jury session on Warner's case.

By mid-March Iosea Hill, 22, described as "from the south," was being held for trial on a charge of killing Mrs. Scranton. According to Prosecutor Young, Hill had confessed, had been removed from the county for safe keeping, and had implicated an Afro-American recently sent to the Mansfield reformatory. No report of a trial or of any arrest of members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

A state survey of Black labor printed on March 1 called Marion "the scene of the recent race trouble" and counted about thirty Black families, property owners, still in the city. Its next lines added that there was no probability of further trouble.

The fullest account in the Black press was a Marion dispatch dated February 5, which the Cleveland Advocate printed on February 8 under the headline "Ohio Is Saved From Lynching Disgrace." The headline stressed the averted lynching, and the dispatch followed the officials' measures closely while reporting the stoning of Black homes and the exodus without comment. On March 1 the Advocate returned to Marion only in passing, within a county-by-county report on Black employment after the war, describing the remaining families as property owners, "some of them" highly respected.

The Cleveland Gazette's March 15 item, printed among other news, reported only the murder charge against Hill, marking Mrs. Scranton as "(white)" and Hill as a newcomer from the South, and said nothing of the attacks on Black residents.

The February dispatch gives two locations for Warner, the Mansfield reformatory and Mount Gilead, and reports threats of lynching against him early Monday while calling him the man arrested "yesterday" in a dispatch dated February 5, which suggests it combined reports from different days.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Marion, Ohio
bases: After a white woman's murder and an assault on another woman, warning placards ordered Black residents to leave Marion by 6 o'clock, a crowd stoned Black homes, and an exodus followed, leaving about thirty Black families in the city (A1, A2, A4).

The detailed account rests on one Marion dispatch in the Cleveland Advocate (A1-A3), but a separate state labor column independently describes 'the recent race trouble' at Marion with about thirty Black families 'still left' (A4), and the Cleveland Gazette independently reports the Scranton murder charge (A6).

accounts.label: Marion dispatch (reprinted in the Cleveland Advocate)
accounts.gist: After the Scranton murder and Christian assault, a crowd gathered on the west side, chased a Black man and stoned Black homes; placards ordered Black residents out and an exodus followed, while vigilantes and officers kept order and moved the accused Warner away from a threatened mob.

accounts.label: Ohio labor column
accounts.gist: Marion was 'the scene of the recent race trouble'; about thirty Black property-owning families remained, and further trouble was not expected.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette item
accounts.gist: Iosea Hill was held for Mrs. Scranton's murder, had confessed according to the prosecutor, and was removed from the county for safe keeping.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate ran a Marion dispatch in the officials' frame under the headline 'Ohio Is Saved From Lynching Disgrace', stressing that no one was lynched while reporting the stoning and the exodus without comment.
A month later the Advocate's labor column called it 'the recent race trouble' and noted that the remaining Black families were property owners, 'some of them' highly respected.
The Cleveland Gazette reported only the murder charge against Hill, identifying the victim as '(white)' and Hill as 'from the south', with no mention of the expulsion.

info: Mrs. Clyde Scranton was killed on the night of Jan. 29, 1919 (a Wednesday night by A1's count).
Marion, Ohio, chiefly its west side and the Erie railroad roundhouse, where many Black men worked.

Black residents of Marion generally: one Black man chased by a crowd, several Black families whose windows were broken, and Black workers ordered to leave; George Washington Warner, accused of the Christian assault, was threatened with lynching.

The crowd assembled after the murder of Mrs. Clyde Scranton and the assault on Mrs. Margaret Christian; Warner was accused of the attack on Mrs. Christian; Iosea Hill was later charged with Mrs. Scranton's murder.
A crowd of men and boys on the west side; unnamed persons who posted warning placards.

Warner was reported in the Mansfield reformatory; Hill was said by the prosecutor to have confessed, was removed from the county, and implicated an Afro-American recently sent to the Mansfield reformatory. No report of a trial was found.
